introduction: Read the complete byte-inspector program before changing it. This guided segment accompanies Chapter 2 and its written lab. Use MIPS64 Release 6 and the Default memory layout. Predict the two interpretations, compare them with actual Run results, then inspect the instruction boundaries in Debug.
conclusion: The five checked runs and the ordered Debug observations now describe the current program. Resume Debug and trace each integer-output argument as the written lab explains. Then investigate the deliberate faults and word-width experiment before attempting the independent output variations. The guided checks do not assess those investigations or independent programs.

steps.explanation: The mask 0xFF has ones in positions 0 through 7. The register still has 64 bits; the AND operation clears the other positions. Assume the supplied instructions are unchanged.
steps.question: How many bit positions can remain nonzero after the mask?

choices.feedback: Only positions 0 through 7 have matching ones in the mask. The other 56 register bits become zero.
The immediate field can encode sixteen bits, but 0xFF contains only eight ones.
The destination remains a 64-bit register, but the mask clears its high 56 bits.

hints.text: Write 0xFF as binary and count the one bits.

steps.explanation: Use input 150. Its low byte is 0x96, or 10010110 in binary. Read the set bits with unsigned place values before interpreting a sign bit.
steps.question: What unsigned value does that byte represent?

choices.feedback: 96 is the pair of hexadecimal digits read as decimal text. In hexadecimal, the high digit contributes 9 times 16.
The set positions contribute 128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 150. The hexadecimal notation describes the same bits.
That is the signed eight-bit interpretation. The unsigned interpretation assigns bit seven weight +128.

hints.text: Start with the contribution of bit seven, then add the lower set bits.
Alternatively, calculate 9 times 16 plus 6.

steps.explanation: The next instruction, seb, sign extends the low byte into the complete register. For 0x96, bit seven is one. Sign extension copies that bit into all higher positions.
steps.question: Which complete value will seb place in t1?

choices.feedback: That is the zero-extended masked value in t0. It does not copy the byte sign bit into the higher positions.
This changes the low-byte pattern. Sign extension preserves those low eight bits.
The low byte remains 0x96 and the upper bits become ones. As a signed 64-bit value, the result is -106.

hints.text: Locate bit seven of the byte, not bit 63 of the masked register.
Keep the final two hexadecimal digits 96. Decide which digit fills every higher position.

steps.explanation: Start a fresh Run of byte-inspector.asm. Enter 150 in its console. Wait for normal completion, then compare the unsigned and signed outputs with your predictions. The lesson checks the integer the program consumed as well as its output.
steps.stdout:
Enter an integer from 0 to 255: Unsigned byte: 150
Signed byte: -106
steps.success: The low byte is 0x96 in both results. Its unsigned value is 150; sign extension preserves its signed-byte value, -106.

hints.text: Use Run on this imported byte-inspector.asm file. Enter the requested decimal integer in the Run console, then let the program finish.
If the input is right but the numbers differ, compare t0 after andi and t1 after seb. A wrong output argument can hide a correct conversion.

steps.explanation: Now consider a fresh launch with input 128. The same two instructions produce the unsigned and signed interpretations in separate registers. The reporting code copies each result into the output argument when it is needed.
steps.question: Which two numbers should the program print for input 128?

choices.feedback: The low byte has bit seven set, so its signed eight-bit interpretation is negative. The second result uses sign extension.
The masked value is 128. Assigning bit seven weight -128 gives the signed value -128, retained by sign extension.
Sign extension changes t1, while the unsigned masked value remains in t0. The first output uses that unchanged value.

hints.text: Trace t0 and t1 separately. A destination written by seb does not replace its source register.

steps.explanation: Start a fresh Run and enter 128. This is the first byte pattern whose sign bit is one. Read both output numbers before continuing.
steps.stdout:
Enter an integer from 0 to 255: Unsigned byte: 128
Signed byte: -128
steps.success: The output changes from unsigned 128 to signed -128. The mask keeps the low byte; seb copies its sign bit into the higher positions.

steps.explanation: Start a fresh Run and enter 0. Decide what the mask and sign extension should do to an all-zero pattern, then compare the two outputs.
steps.stdout:

Signed byte: 0
steps.success: Both values are zero. This checks the all-zero pattern, but it does not distinguish sign extension from a plain copy.

steps.explanation: Start a fresh Run and enter 127. This pattern sets every low bit except bit seven. Compare the unsigned and signed outputs and explain why they agree.
steps.stdout:
Enter an integer from 0 to 255: Unsigned byte: 127
Signed byte: 127
steps.success: Both values are 127 because bit seven is zero. A faulty plain copy would also pass this case; the negative cases are necessary.

steps.explanation: Start a fresh Run and enter 255. All eight low bits are one. Compare both outputs, then explain why interpreting the second value as signed produces -1.
steps.stdout:
Enter an integer from 0 to 255: Unsigned byte: 255
Signed byte: -1
steps.success: The unsigned result is 255 and the signed result is -1. Together with the other runs, this exposes faults that positive-only examples miss.

steps.explanation: Stop any earlier Debug session. Put a line breakpoint on andi under interpret, then launch Debug for this imported byte-inspector.asm. Enter 150 in its console. The lesson checks three ordered pauses in one fresh forward session. If you edit registers or memory, or use Backstep while exploring, start another Debug session to record these observations.

stops.explanation: Pause on andi under interpret. Input has completed, but the highlighted mask instruction has not executed. In the Debug register view, inspect all sixteen hexadecimal digits of v0: 0x0000000000000096. That is the input 150 before the mask. Wait for this observation to advance before stepping.
stops.success: At this boundary v0 contains the input. The mask is still the next instruction, so this pause does not yet show its effect.

hints.text: Click the editor gutter beside andi below interpret. Use Debug on this file, then enter 150 in that session’s console.
If Debug is already on seb, andi has executed. Start a fresh Debug session to observe the earlier boundary first.

stops.explanation: Use Step Over once. Debug should now highlight seb. Inspect t0 as 0x0000000000000096 and v0 as 0x0000000000000096. The mask has written t0; it has not overwritten the input register. These values are measured before seb executes.
stops.success: The mask retained the low eight bits and cleared t0’s upper 56 bits. The selected input already had zero upper bits, so v0 and t0 currently agree.

hints.text: Read the highlighted instruction as the next operation. When seb is next, the preceding andi has completed.

stops.explanation: Use Step Over once more. Debug should highlight the first la under report. Inspect t0 as 0x0000000000000096 and t1 as 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF96. Compare the upper digits as well as the shared low byte 96. The reporting code has not yet consumed either result.
stops.success: The byte sign bit was one. seb copied it into t1’s upper 56 positions while retaining the low byte. As a signed 64-bit value, t1 is -106; t0 remains unsigned 150.

hints.text: 0x00000000FFFFFF96 is not the expected 64-bit result. Sign extension must also fill the highest eight hexadecimal digits with F.

steps.success: You have observed the input, the completed mask and the completed sign extension at distinct boundaries. Resume this Debug session and use the written lab to trace the output arguments.

hints.text: Use the Debug register view, not console output alone. Service 1 prints a signed 32-bit value and cannot show every bit of a 64-bit register.
